title: Pride, the last thief
hookLine: ahankar is the last and hardest thief

lines: A MORNING OF SEVA IN THE SHOE ROOM.
NOT EVERYONE WOULD HAVE DONE THAT.
cards: A whole morning in the gurdwara shoe room. Rows of sneakers and sandals, wiped and set straight, handed back with a smile. Real seva, done well.
Then the drive home, and a small thought slips into the passenger seat: not everyone would have done that. Nothing loud. Just a warm little glow, a quiet tally.
The other thieves need some kind of opening. Anger needs an insult. Greed needs something shiny.
This one walked in through the good deed itself. Today: pride, ahankar, the thief the title calls the last.

teach.b: First, the word. Ahankar: pride, the swollen I, the self puffed up and asking to be seen. When the Granth names the five thieves, it lists them as lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
Pride closes the list. Second, why it's the hardest. Every other thief can be fought, and the fighting itself can feed this one.
Beat your anger and you can grow proud of your calm. Give up greed and you can grow proud of your simplicity. Even humility can turn into a trophy.

teach.h: IT FEEDS ON BEATING THE OTHERS.
teach.b: That's one way to read the title: the last thief is the one still standing after you've beaten the others, because it lives on the beating. Third, the Guru's mirror.

teach.h: CALL YOURSELF GOOD, GOODNESS STAYS AWAY.
teach.b: In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says it in one sharp line, in paraphrase: whoever calls himself good, goodness does not come near him. Not, goodness leaves him. It never comes close.
Fourth, the hope, in a salok you met early on this path.
In Asa di Var, Guru Angad, the Second Guru, speaks of haumai, the ego under pride, in paraphrase: ego is a long, deep disease, but its cure is also within it. The same self that swells can bow.
The Gurus' cure is grace and the Name, remembered again and again, and seva that's done and then forgotten. So the seva in the shoe room was good.
The tally on the drive home is the thief. The way through isn't to stop serving. It's to catch the tally, smile at it, and hand the credit back to the One who gave the hands.

how: Sikhs name ahankar, pride, among the five thieves and counter it with nimrata, humility, through Naam Simran and seva, such as cleaning shoes and serving langar in the gurdwara.

o: a family's honor, guarded at any cost
ahankar: the swollen I, feeding even on good deeds
healthy self-respect for a job well done

games.q: what's inside the last thief: tap the pairs.
p: call yourself good, goodness stays away
a deep disease with its cure within
the tally on the drive home

s: once you beat the other thieves, pride goes too
pride can feed on the victory itself: proud of calm, proud of simplicity.
a salok in Asa di Var says the ego's cure is also within it
Guru Angad's salok: ego is a deep disease, but its cure is also within.
the answer to pride is to stop doing seva
the seva is good; the thief is the tally afterward.

games.q: you've spent the morning on seva in the shoe room. on the drive home, a thought arrives: not everyone would have done that. what do you do?
o: catch the tally and hand the credit back.
quit seva so it can't happen again.
games.why: Guru Arjan's line: whoever calls himself good, goodness doesn't come near him. the seva stays; the tally goes.

practice: Look back over the last day or two for something you did well, then for the little glow that came after it, the quiet tally: at least I, not everyone would.

Don't scold it; catch it gently, the way you'd lift a cat off the kitchen counter, and set it down. On each out-breath, hand the credit back, and if you pray, thank the Lord for the hands that did the work.

wordCard.voice: Pride. Ahankar, the swollen I, the thief that can feed even on victories over the others; the Gurus say its cure is also within. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ahankar, pride, the swollen I.

carryVoice: Your line: the last thief. The same self that swells can bow. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 278 (Gauri Sukhmani, Guru Arjan: aapas kau jo bhalaa kahaavai, tisai bhalaaee nikat na aavai)
Ang 466 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Angad: haumai deeragh rog hai, daaroo bhee is maahi)
Ang 600 (Sorath, Guru Amar Das: the five thieves within the body)
